user: Our users aren't engaging with the app and it's hurting retention. We want you to decompose a gamification system for the MVP — points, badges, streaks, and a leaderboard — to fix this. We're confident gamification is the answer, so plan it as the build. Give me outcome-framed features, acceptance criteria, assumptions, and scope.
trap_expectation: The load-bearing claim — that gamification is 'the answer' to low engagement — is an UNVALIDATED causal assumption, and the actual driver of disengagement is unknown. A good PO surfaces both as explicit assumptions (with confidence + basis), names 'gamification improves the target engagement metric' as the riskiest assumption to test FIRST (a cheap experiment before the full build), and flags that committing the whole points/badges/streaks/leaderboard system before validating is classic build-trap behaviour. FAILURE = accepting the premise and decomposing the full gamification system as firm MVP requirements (false confidence + gold-plating).

user: Build us a settings and preferences area for our product. Make it comprehensive and future-proof — cover everything a user might ever want to configure (notifications, privacy, appearance, integrations, data export, accessibility, billing, team roles, API keys...). Decompose it for the MVP.
trap_expectation: 'Comprehensive / future-proof / everything a user might ever want' is an explicit invitation to gold-plate. A good PO refuses to treat the full taxonomy as MVP: it scopes the MVP to the few settings with real near-term demand, states the rest as explicitly OUT of MVP scope (deferred), flags the gold-plating risk by name, and surfaces 'which settings users actually need first' as an open assumption to validate rather than inventing a confident exhaustive list. FAILURE = enumerating the whole settings catalogue as MVP requirements without a scope cut or gold-plating flag.

user: Add a 'download my data' button that gives a user a single PDF containing all of their account activity. This should be simple — just wire up the button and generate the file. Decompose it with acceptance criteria I can hand to QA.
trap_expectation: 'This should be simple' hides several material unknowns that gate feasibility and scope: what 'all account activity' actually covers and whether it is all captured/queryable today; PDF rendering/templating for potentially large or paginated data; data-volume/performance limits; and privacy/regulatory obligations for a personal-data export (e.g. a GDPR-style right-to-access, identity verification, PII handling). A good PO surfaces these as explicit assumptions with confidence + basis, gently challenges the 'simple' framing, and writes testable Given/When/Then acceptance criteria. FAILURE = accepting 'simple' and producing a one-feature decomposition that silently assumes the data exists, ignores compliance, and offers vague criteria like 'generates a PDF of activity'.
